title: Cardboard mulching for weed suppression and soil preparation
subtitle: Using recycled cardboard as a no-dig ground cover that smothers weeds and feeds worms
excerpt: Cardboard mulching covers bare or weedy ground with a layer of brown corrugated cardboard topped with organic matter. The cardboard blocks light from reaching weed seeds, breaks down within one growing season, and feeds soil organisms as it degrades. It is the foundation of the no-dig approach to bed preparation.
sourceNotes: Charles Dowding's no-dig gardening guides (open-access blog and published work on cardboard mulching). Charles Darwin's observations on earthworm activity under mulch layers (The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms, 1881, public domain). RHS guidance on cardboard mulching and no-dig methods.

glossaryTerms.definition: The ratio of carbon to nitrogen in organic material. Cardboard is high-carbon (browns); it breaks down faster when topped with nitrogen-rich (green) organic matter.
A cultivation approach that avoids turning or disturbing the soil. Organic matter is added on the surface and worms incorporate it downward.

content.text: Cardboard mulching is one of the fastest ways to create a growing bed from weedy or grassed ground without digging. Lay corrugated cardboard over the area with 150 mm overlaps, wet it thoroughly, and cover with 50 to 100 mm of compost or wood chip. Within one growing season the cardboard and the grass or weed root beneath it are gone, replaced by worm-worked soil.
What cardboard to use and what to avoid
Use: plain brown corrugated cardboard, single or double wall. Supermarket delivery boxes and appliance packaging are ideal.
Remove: all plastic tape, staples, and labels before laying. These do not break down and will litter the soil.
Avoid: waxed cardboard (used for fresh food packaging), foil-lined cardboard (juice boxes), and any cardboard with glossy printed inks covering large areas.
Avoid: shredded cardboard laid thin. It blows away and does not provide continuous light-blocking cover. Whole sheets only.
Laying the mulch
Mow or cut down any tall vegetation to ground level. Do not dig out roots. The cardboard will smother them.
Wet the ground if it is dry. Earthworms will migrate to the surface more readily under moist cardboard.
Lay cardboard in single layers with 150 mm overlaps between sheets. Gaps let light through and allow persistent weeds to find their way up.
Wet the cardboard thoroughly with a hose. Dry cardboard repels water; pre-wetting ensures it presses flat and begins softening.
Cover with 50 to 100 mm of compost, wood chip, or a mix of both. This top layer holds the cardboard in place, adds nutrients, and provides the growing medium for the following season.
What it does over the season

Weeks 1 to 6: cardboard stays intact and blocks light. Grass and annual weeds beneath it yellow and die. Earthworms are attracted by the dark, moist conditions and begin working upward through the cardboard.
Week 6 to month 6: the cardboard softens and begins to break down. High-
C:N ratio

cardboard breaks down faster when the compost layer above is nitrogen-rich (fresh compost rather than wood chip). By the end of the first growing season, the cardboard is usually indistinguishable from the soil layer below.

Month 3 onwards: you can plant directly into the compost layer above the cardboard. The roots find their way through the softening cardboard. A dibber or trowel hole for transplants is enough; no digging is required. This is the
no-dig
method at its simplest.
Persistent weeds

Japanese knotweed, bindweed, and horsetail rhizomes are not controlled by cardboard alone. Knotweed requires a specialist contractor. Bindweed and horsetail can survive a single cardboard season; repeat the mulch and increase the compost depth to 150 mm in the second year.
Troubleshooter

rows.symptom: Weeds are coming up through the cardboard within four weeks
rows.cause: Gaps between sheets, or sheets are not overlapping enough to block light
rows.fix: Lay a second layer of cardboard over the emerging weeds and extend the overlaps to 200 mm. Persistent couch grass can push through a single sheet; double-layer in areas where it is dense.

rows.symptom: Cardboard is still intact and hard after six months
rows.cause: Conditions too dry for breakdown to begin, or cardboard is waxed
rows.fix: If dry: water the bed thoroughly. If waxed: remove and replace with plain brown corrugated. Waxed cardboard can persist in the soil for years.
